source.version: NBER Working Paper 33641, April 2025 (PDF pp. 1-2), titled '...Generative AI Reshaping Teamwork and Expertise'. This is not the latest version. The latest is the Organization Science 2026 article (doi 10.1287/orsc.2025.20702, titled '...on Generative AI and Teamwork'), which is not on file. The search record says its abstract reports N = 791; this version's text says 776. The retrieval entry has no version_saved field. PDF page numbers equal the printed page numbers.
source.title_on_document: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI Reshaping Teamwork and Expertise

supplement.where: Appendix A-C and Figure A1, pp. 47-54 of this PDF. This is the 'Appendix' the footnotes cite: fn. 5 sends readers there for the tasks, which are printed on p. 47. No separate online supplement is named.
supplement.holds: Problem statements (App. A, p. 47); evaluation process and inter-rater reliability (App. B, pp. 48-49: 22 evaluators, 1,595 evaluations of 550 solutions, 2.89 per solution, ICC2 0.452); prompts (App. C, pp. 50-53); solution length by arm (Figure A1, p. 54). Footnote 11 (p. 13) says the replication with AI-generated evaluations is 'shown in Appendix', but no such result appears in this PDF. Novelty, feasibility, impact, and business-potential results are not printed anywhere in this PDF. No statistic needed for extraction sits only in the appendix.

paper_design_summary: Between May and July 2024, Procter & Gamble Commercial and R&D professionals in a preregistered one-day virtual product-development workshop were randomly assigned in a 2x2 design to work alone or in a randomly paired cross-functional two-person team, with or without a GPT-4-based tool and one hour of prompt training. Each individual or team submitted one solution to a real business-unit innovation problem. Blind evaluators rated the 550 solutions on overall quality (the primary outcome), novelty, feasibility, impact, business potential, and technical orientation, and the paper also reports solution length, time spent, a top-10-percent quality indicator, embedding similarity across solutions (figure only), and self-reported emotions.

studies.label: P&G product-development field experiment (2x2: alone or in a two-person team, with or without a GPT-4-based tool)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual participants, within eight strata (four business units by two geographies), to one of four conditions: Individual No AI (Control), Team No AI (T1), Individual + AI (T2), Team + AI (T3). Team arms were formed by randomly pairing one Commercial and one R&D professional, and one randomly designated member shared the screen and submitted. AI arms got the GPT-4-based tool and one hour of prompt training. After the initial task, both no-AI groups got the training and repeated the task with AI (crossover). All reported results use only the initial between-subject task.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to these conditions within each of the eight randomization clusters, defined by four business units (Baby Care, Feminine Care, Grooming, and Oral Care) across two geographies (Europe and Americas).
assignment.locator: p. 9, Section 3.2; p. 10, Section 3.2 (stratification, random pairing, fn. 8 reassignment); p. 11, Section 3.3 (crossover); p. 29, Figure 1
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 2 (AEA RCT Registry trials/13603); p. 8, footnote 3 (AEARCTR-0013603; plan public upon acceptance or after the registry embargo)

arms.name: Individual No AI (Control)
arms.description: Works alone without AI on the scored initial task. Gets the AI training only afterward (crossover, no results reported).

arms.name: Team No AI (T1)
arms.description: Randomly paired R&D + Commercial two-person team working together over Microsoft Teams without AI; 115 teams. The human partner is the aid.

arms.name: Individual + AI (T2)
arms.description: Works alone with the GPT-4-based tool after a one-hour prompt training and a PDF of recommended prompts.

arms.name: Team + AI (T3)
arms.description: Randomly paired R&D + Commercial two-person team with the GPT-4-based tool after the same training; 126 teams.

participants.exclusions: 811 people took part in the workshop (p. 9). 35 of them were not randomly assigned: late entrants did the task alone without AI, and staff above seniority band 3 did it alone with AI (p. 9, fn. 6). The text says the analyses focus on the 776 participants who were randomly assigned (p. 9, and 776 again on pp. 2 and 4), which leaves all 35 out, and fn. 6 says results are consistent when they are included. Table 1 (p. 41) lists 154 + 155 individuals and 230 (115 teams) + 252 (126 teams) team participants, and their units make up exactly the 550 solutions in Tables 2-4 and 10 (154 + 155 + 115 + 126). The PDF never prints the total of these counts. n_analyzed = 791 is the sum of the four printed arm counts. The two totals cannot both describe the analyzed sample. If 791 of the 811 were analyzed, only 20 were left out, so at least 15 of the 35 non-randomized participants, who all worked alone, sit in the individual arms. If all 35 were left out, at most 776 were analyzed, and Table 1 counts 15 people beyond them. The document does not say which holds. Also, if one member of a team failed to participate, the team was nullified and the other member was moved to an individual assignment. The number moved, and whether they kept their AI condition, are not stated (p. 10, fn. 8). So the paper gives no count at assignment, n_randomized is null, and the analysis is not intention-to-treat. The emotion outcomes use 533 and 530 observations (Tables 6-7, p. 44).
participants.who: Experienced Commercial and R&D professionals at Procter & Gamble in four business units (Baby Care, Feminine Care, Grooming, Oral Care), enrolled through an organizational upskilling initiative
participants.country: Not stated by country; two geographies, Europe and Americas
participants.quote: The experiment was conducted as a one-day virtual product development workshop, involving 811 participants from P&G’s Commercial and R&D functions. Our analyses focus on 776 of these participants who were randomly assigned across four conditions.
participants.locator: p. 9, Section 3.2 and fn. 6; p. 2, Abstract and p. 4, Section 1 (776); p. 10, fn. 8; per-arm counts p. 41, Table 1; 550 observations p. 42, Table 2

ai_tool.name_model: GenAI tool built on GPT-4, accessed through Microsoft Azure; participants at the July workshop had GPT-4o (p. 10, fn. 10)
ai_tool.how_used: AI arms got a one-hour training session, led by one of the authors, on prompting the tool for CPG tasks, plus a PDF of recommended prompts (research, consumer simulation, problem framing, ideation, selection, simulated customer interviews; Appendix C, pp. 50-53). They then used the tool 'as they saw fit' (p. 50). In teams, one randomly designated member shared the screen and submitted the solution (p. 10). All prompts and responses were recorded (p. 11).

task.description: Develop a new solution (new products, packaging, communication approaches, or retail execution) to a real innovation problem of the participant's own business unit. The four problem statements are in Appendix A (p. 47). Each submission had five parts: idea name, recommended solution, rationale, critical work required, and support or resources needed (p. 48, App. B.2).
task.duration: One-day virtual workshop sessions held between May and July 2024. No fixed task time limit is stated. Time spent is an outcome (Table 4, p. 43, log seconds).

outcomes.name: Solution quality (standardized)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Overall Quality on a 1-10 scale ('A comprehensive assessment of the solution's merit', App. B.3, p. 48), rated by evaluators blind to condition and submitter. The 22 evaluators are called experts; they were MBA and engineering students or recent graduates at a top business or engineering school (App. B.1). 1,595 evaluations of 550 solutions, 2.89 per solution (App. B.4, p. 49; p. 13 says 'more than three'), ICC2 0.452. Ratings averaged per solution and standardized on the Individual No AI group. OLS with one row per solution and robust SEs: Model 1 treatment indicators only, Model 2 business-unit and date fixed effects, Model 3 adds controls (band, tenure, gender, prior AI use). Distributions in Figure 3 (p. 31). Heterogeneity by core vs non-core job in Table 5 (p. 43) and Figure 5. Robustness variant with no printed numbers: a replication with AI-generated evaluations (fn. 11, p. 13). Novelty, feasibility, impact, and business potential are listed as separate outcomes (S1-O2, S1-O5 to S1-O7).

outcomes.name: Novelty (expert rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Novelty on a 1-10 scale ('the degree of innovation and originality', p. 13; 'The originality and uniqueness of the approach', App. B.3, p. 48), rated by the same blind evaluators in the same evaluation pass as quality. The paper calls it a robustness check. No estimate, mean, test, or figure is printed in this PDF. The only result statement is the blanket sentence that novelty, feasibility, and impact 'confirm the findings reported in the main text' (pp. 10-11). It names no arm and no direction, so no contrast is recorded, as for business potential (S1-O7).

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity between solutions (distance from condition mean)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Kernel densities, by condition, of each solution's 'Distance from Mean (Squared Units)' in sentence-embedding space. The figure note says the cosine distance between solutions is calculated and that lower values mean higher similarity. Figure only. The axis is a distance, so lower values mean less diversity. The text reports higher similarity with AI, which is lower diversity (sign reversed from similarity). Figure 13 also plots an 'AI Only' set of GPT-4o solutions (fn. 14). No participant produced them, so that comparison is recorded separately as S1-O10 (question none).

contrasts.reported: Density plot only; no means, sample sizes, SEs, or tests. Text: 'AI-aided solutions demonstrate notably higher semantic similarity.' Read off the figure (approximate, not printed): Alone + AI peaks at about 0.6, Alone at about 0.7. Sign reversed: higher similarity means lower diversity.

Density plot only; no means, sample sizes, SEs, or tests. Same text as the row above. Read off the figure (approximate, not printed): Pair + AI peaks at about 0.6, Pair at about 0.7. Sign reversed: higher similarity means lower diversity.

Density plot only; no means, sample sizes, SEs, or tests. The text sets both human-only conditions ('both individual and pair') against the AI-aided ones. Read off the figure (approximate, not printed): Alone + AI peaks at about 0.6, Pair at about 0.7.

outcomes.name: Technicality of solution (technical vs commercial orientation)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Technical versus commercial orientation, a 1-7 Likert rating by the same blind evaluators (higher = more technically oriented). An orientation measure, not a creativity rating. It is recorded because it is scored on the output and the paper reads it as breadth of expertise. Reported only as densities: by Commercial vs R&D background within each individual arm (Figure 6) and by team arm (Figure 11, with bimodality coefficients). The p. 16 text places commercial participants at higher x-axis values and calls them green, while Section 4.2 and the Figure 6 note define higher values as more technical and say blue. The paper says quality did not vary significantly with technical orientation (p. 16, no numbers).

contrasts.reported: Densities by background within each arm, with no arm-level means or tests. 'mixed' means the AI effect differs by background, not that it differs in sign. With AI, Commercial is at about 3.69 and R&D at about 3.82. The gap closes because Commercial solutions become more technical. The R&D line does not move, although the R&D density peak shifts from about 5.2 to about 4.8. Text: without AI, participants generated ideas 'closely aligned with their professional backgrounds', and with AI 'this distinction largely disappeared'. company_involvement.description: The experiment ran inside Procter & Gamble on real business-unit problems, and the design was tailored with P&G leadership. Four co-authors (Yi Han, Jeff Goldman, Hari Nair, Stewart Taub) list P&G affiliations. P&G gave financial support to the Digital Data Design Institute at Harvard Business School through gifts in 2023-2025, and Karim Lakhani was paid as a P&G consultant in 2021-2022. The AI tool is described only as built on GPT-4 and accessed through Microsoft Azure. The document states no role for an AI company.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1 (acknowledgments); p. 2 (affiliations); p. 8, Section 3.1; p. 10, Section 3.2

eligibility.reason: Professionals were randomly assigned, stratified by business unit and geography, to work with or without a GPT-4-based tool, crossed with working alone or in a randomly paired two-person team, on a product-idea task (pp. 9-10). People analyzed: 791 as the sum of the four Table 1 arm counts (p. 41, a total the PDF never prints) and 776 per the text (pp. 2, 4, 9). Both are far above 50, and the two individual arms alone hold 154 and 155 people. Blind evaluators scored each submitted solution (quality, the paper's primary outcome, Table 2), and Figure 13 compares embedding distances across solutions (figure only). AI was available while the scored solutions were produced, in the initial task before the control groups' crossover (p. 11). Caveats: the primary outcome is overall quality (usefulness), not a creativity rating. Novelty was rated, but no novelty result is printed in this version. If Table 1's 791 people are the analyzed sample, at least 15 of the 35 non-randomized participants sit in the individual arms, and the paper does not say which total is right (p. 9, fn. 6; p. 41). An unstated number of team members were moved to individual arms after a partner did not take part (p. 10, fn. 8). None of these caveats changes a criterion.

one_line_finding: Individuals randomly assigned a GPT-4-based tool produced solutions rated 0.373 control-group SD higher in overall quality than individuals without AI (SE 0.106; Table 2, p. 42), about the level of two-person teams without AI, while teams with AI did not differ significantly from teams without AI (p = 0.242, Table 2) and AI-aided solutions were more semantically similar to each other (Figure 13, p. 40, figure only).
open_questions: People analyzed: the text gives 776 professionals (pp. 2, 4) and says the analyses focus on 776 randomly assigned participants (p. 9), but the Table 1 arm counts (154, 155, 230, 252) sum to 791 and match the 550 solutions. The document does not explain the gap. If 791 is the analyzed sample, at least 15 of the 35 non-randomized participants are in the individual arms (811 - 791 = 20 left out). The Organization Science 2026 version reportedly reports 791. Does it explain the change, and does it say whether non-randomized participants were analyzed?
Footnote 8 (p. 10): members of incomplete teams were moved to individual assignments after randomization. The number moved, and whether they kept their AI condition, are not stated.

Novelty, feasibility, impact, and the AI-generated evaluations are said to confirm the results (p. 11; fn. 11, p. 13), but no statistics appear in this PDF, and business potential has no result at all. This form records no contrast for novelty, feasibility, impact, or business potential, because the blanket sentence names no arm and no direction. Check the Organization Science version and any online appendix for these results.

Figure 13 gives no numbers, sample sizes, or tests for the similarity comparison, and its note describes the measure two ways. A diversity effect needs the journal version, posted data, or the authors.

Primary record: the paper's primary outcome is overall quality, a usefulness rating, not a creativity rating. Is it acceptable as this paper's with_ai record when novelty was rated but not reported here? Also, the two ai_vs_bau quality contrasts use different control arms, and Team + AI vs Team No AI has only a p-value for the difference (no SE).
The paper calls its 22 evaluators experts, but they were MBA and engineering students or recent graduates (App. B.1, p. 48). The record uses expert_raters, following the paper's description.
Codebook gap for Review 1: no measure code fits a plain word count (solution length). The record uses automated_score, as the other reconciled forms do for word counts.
notes: Version on file is NBER WP 33641 (April 2025). The latest version is the 2026 Organization Science article, not on file. The unit of analysis is the solution: one per individual and one per team, so each team observation stands for two people. Regressions have one row per solution with robust SEs. Outcomes not listed because they are not scored on the output or answer none of the three questions: log time on task (Table 4, p. 43; Figure 4), self-reported positive and negative emotions (Tables 6-9, pp. 44-45; Figures 7-8), expected top-10% placement (self-report, Figure 10, p. 38), and the AI-content retention rate (Figure 12, p. 39; AI arms only). Control groups repeated the task with AI after training (crossover, p. 11). No crossover results are reported and no output is produced after AI was removed, so the paper answers with_ai and across_people only. Individual + AI vs Team No AI (ai_vs_active) is coded for quality, similarity, and length, where the text compares those arms. Table 10 would also allow it for top 10% (0.019 vs 0.037 against the same baseline), but the paper neither tests nor discusses it, so it is not coded. It is not coded for technicality because the p. 21 discussion (teams without AI 'produced more balanced solutions') conflicts with Section 6.3 (teams without AI are bimodal). Rewards for the best proposals were set within each treatment group (p. 11). Other document inconsistencies: 'more than three' evaluations per solution (p. 13) vs 2.89 (p. 49); the p. 16 text reverses the technicality axis and the color relative to Section 4.2 and the Figure 6 note; the p. 19 text says GPT-4o was prompted 'iteratively' while fn. 14 says 'with no additional iterations'; Section 4.1 (p. 12) points to 'section 3.2 below' for the outcome definitions, which are in Section 4.2. The Model 1 Control Mean in Table 2 is 0.000 by construction, because quality is standardized on the control group. The (0.081) under it is not labeled. It matches 1/sqrt(154) = 0.081, the standard error of a mean with SD 1 over 154 people. It is not the control-group SD, which is 1 by construction. S1-O10 records the Figure 13 'AI Only' comparison as context (question none), because no participant produced the GPT-4o solutions. Assignment caveats that change no code: Table 1 (p. 41) shows the AI split balanced within each format, but the individual arms hold more R&D staff (0.604 and 0.594) than the team arms (0.500 by construction) and have longer tenure (12.351 and 11.816 vs 10.091 and 10.476 years). The paper does not say how the split into individual and team arms handled function. This bears on the Individual + AI vs Team No AI rows, not on the AI contrasts. The paper also describes no check that the no-AI arms did not use AI on their own, and 71 to 81 percent of each arm had ChatGPT access at work (Table 1, p. 41).

open_items.item: People analyzed (open question 1 and the open people-lens problem): the text gives 776 (pp. 2, 4, 9), while the Table 1 arm counts sum to 791 and match the 550 solutions. If 791 is right, at least 15 of the 35 non-randomized participants sit in the individual arms. Criterion 2 holds under either total. Criterion 1 holds because the design randomizes and fn. 6 says results are consistent when the non-randomized participants are included. The Organization Science abstract reportedly gives 791. If the journal version does not explain the gap, the authors.

Reassignment after randomization (open question 2): the number of team members moved to individual arms after a partner did not take part, and whether they kept their AI condition, are not stated (p. 10, fn. 8). This bears on arm composition, not on whether AI was randomly assigned.

Novelty, feasibility, impact, business potential, and the AI-generated evaluations (open question 3): this PDF prints no result for them, so no contrast is coded. Criterion 3 rests on quality (Table 2) and similarity (Figure 13), not on these ratings. Novelty numbers would add a secondary with_ai record on the construct closest to creativity.

Figure 13 similarity (open question 4): no numbers, sample sizes, or tests, and the note describes the measure two ways. A diversity effect for S1-O3, and numbers for the S1-O10 context rows, need the underlying scores. If the journal version does not print them, the authors.

Primary record (open question 5): the paper names overall quality, a usefulness rating, as its primary outcome, so codebook section 8 rule 1 makes it the with_ai primary record. The two ai_vs_bau quality contrasts use different control arms, and Team + AI vs Team No AI has a printed p-value but no SE for the difference. Both are extraction matters.

Rater code (open question 6): the paper calls its 22 evaluators experts, but they were MBA and engineering students or recent graduates (App. B.1, p. 48). The record uses expert_raters. Review 1 may prefer human_raters.

Word-count measure code (open question 7 and the rejected outcome-lens problem): no codebook measure fits solution length, and the record uses automated_score, as the other forms do. This is a Review 1 codebook decision.
